description: We’re a friendly and diverse team where everyone brings a unique set of skills. From science and technology to creativity, design, and communication, we combine our strengths, support each other, and turn different ideas into one great result
summary: Fire Calendar is a free web tool that turns 25 years of satellite fire detections into one consistent, easy-to-read record. Our challenge was Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. These sensors count fires very differently: in 2019, VIIRS reported about 3.3× more detections than MODIS over the same country. Because of that, raw counts from 2005 and 2022 can’t be compared, and an apparent “increase” may just be a new satellite. We calibrated every sensor to a single MODIS-equivalent scale using the 174 months when both generations observed Kazakhstan together (Terra-only × 2.05, VIIRS × 0.306). The calibrated series agrees with MODIS at a monthly correlation of 0.98. Users pick any area and get a year-by-month calendar showing how each month differs from the multi-year norm, for example October 2026 at −70%. This gives emergency services, scientists and land managers a reliable answer to one practical question: is this fire season normal or alarming?
details:
What it does and how it works:

We processed 3.9 million active-fire detections from NASA FIRMS: MODIS Terra and Aqua (C6.1) and VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20 (375 m, C2).

Filtering: we dropped low-confidence detections and masked static heat sources such as gas flares and industrial plants, which left 3.1 million.

Gridding: we counted detections per 0.25° grid cell (4,917 cells) and per month, storing each sensor’s own count side by side.

Calibration: we merged everything into one MODIS-equivalent series from 2001 to today. Terra-only data (2001–2002) is scaled by 2.05, Terra + Aqua is the reference level, and VIIRS is scaled by 0.306. We derived the factors from 174 months of overlap.

In the web app, the user selects an area on the map or by coordinates and sees a year × month calendar colored by deviation from the norm: blue is quieter than usual, red is stronger. Clicking a month shows its value, the norm and the per-sensor counts. Results export as CSV and PNG, and the interface is available in Russian and English. User can also see the expected activity and see the latest updates every 3-6 hours.

Benefits and intended impact:

Early-warning and emergency teams: see in seconds whether the current month is unusual for their area.

Scientists: get a homogeneous, validated 25-year series instead of a record broken by sensor changes.

Land managers and local authorities: learn when their local fire peak arrives (nationally, April holds about 20% of yearly detections) and plan prevention.

The method relies only on global NASA FIRMS data, so it can be reused for other countries.

Tools and technologies:

Data: NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time active-fire data.

Web app: a static site in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server and no install, hosted on GitHub

Presentation: HTML, CSS 3D and JavaScript Canvas, with an interactive 3D terrain built from our real grid data.

Creativity

Instead of another fire map, we built a “fire calendar”: 26 years of history fit on one screen, and a reader sees anomalies at a glance without any GIS skills. Our pitch deck is itself built from the project’s real data. Every column in 2D or 3D is an actual grid cell, and the deck replays all 25 years live.

Factors we considered:

Scientific honesty: we validated the calibration (r = 0.98) and state its limits openly. There is one country-wide coefficient, a detection is not a confirmed fire, and the latest months use near-real-time data that NASA later replaces.

Accessibility: the tool is free, open source, bilingual and runs in anywhere.

Clear visual design: deviation from the norm is shown with a diverging blue-to-red color scale.
